title: Query data using SELECT, WHERE, and LIKE
summary: Builds a world_food table in pgAdmin from a CSV, then works through progressively more selective SELECT queries: all rows, one column, several columns, WHERE with comparison operators, and pattern matching with LIKE, % and the || concatenation operator.

concepts.heading: Setting up the practice data
points: Dataset: world-food.csv, nine countries with rice and wheat production for 2021 in million metric tons. It lives in the existing database called world.
Table spec: id (SERIAL, PRIMARY KEY), country (VARCHAR(45)), rice_production (FLOAT), wheat_production (FLOAT). FLOAT is the new type here; it stores numbers with decimals.
Write the CREATE TABLE in the pgAdmin Query tool. Columns sit inside parentheses, separated by commas, with no comma after the last column, and the statement ends with a semicolon.
After running it, refresh the Tables node to see world_food. Viewing all rows at this point shows an empty grid.
Import: right-click the table, choose Import/Export Data, pick the CSV, keep Import (not Export) selected, and switch on Header in Options.
The CSV has no id column, so remove id from the 'Columns to import' list. SERIAL then generates ids 1 to 9 automatically.

concepts.heading: SELECT: choosing columns
points: SELECT * FROM table returns every row and every column. The asterisk means 'all columns'.
SELECT column FROM table isolates one column, e.g. one phone-number column from a customers table.
SELECT col1, col2 FROM table returns several columns; separate the names with commas, no trailing comma before FROM.
The general shape so far: SELECT (what columns) FROM (which table).

concepts.heading: WHERE: filtering rows
points: WHERE goes after the FROM clause and keeps only the rows whose condition is true.
Equality uses a single = sign (unlike JavaScript's == or ===). String values need single quotes in SQL: WHERE country = 'United States'.
The column you filter on does not have to be the column you select, so one query can look up one cell of data (e.g. a user's credit balance by username).
Comparison operators work as in other languages: <, >, <=, >=, plus = for equality.
Exercise results: US rice production is 8.7; countries with wheat_production > 20 give a reduced list.

concepts.heading: LIKE: fuzzy matching
points: = only matches an exact value, so 'United States' would miss a stored 'United States of America'. LIKE matches against a pattern instead.
% is the wildcard standing for any run of characters (including none).
|| is the string concatenation operator in Postgres, not a logical OR as in many languages. 'U' || '%' builds the pattern 'U%'.
'U%' matches values that start with U (Ukraine, United States). '%a' matches values ending in a (Australia, China, Ethiopia, India).
Writing the pattern as a literal ('U%') works the same. The || form matters later when the value is a variable or expression coming from backend code and must be joined to the wildcard.
Pattern matching is easy to get too broad: 'United%' would also match United Kingdom.

task.name: World food queries
task.starting_point: world-food.csv from the lesson resources and the existing world database in pgAdmin.
task.goal: Create and fill world_food, then write each query listed in the steps.
steps: Create world_food with id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, country VARCHAR(45), rice_production FLOAT, wheat_production FLOAT.
Import the CSV with Header on and the id column excluded; confirm nine rows.
Get the rice production of the United States (single value, 8.7).
List countries whose wheat production is greater than 20.
List countries starting with U (Ukraine, United States) using LIKE and ||.
List countries ending in a (Australia, China, Ethiopia, India).
task.expected_result: Each query returns the reduced result grid described above.
task.reference_repo_path: Section 33 - PostgreSQL/33.07 - Query data using SELECT, WHERE, and LIKE/README.md

pitfalls: Leaving id in the import column list when the CSV has no id values.
Trailing comma after the last column in CREATE TABLE.
Using double quotes around string values (Postgres treats them as identifiers); use single quotes.
Reading || as OR; it concatenates strings.
Using = when only part of the value is known.

gaps_and_ideas: New lesson 'Querying with SELECT, WHERE and LIKE': blurb on reading and filtering rows.
Tasks: select all, select columns, WHERE with a comparison, LIKE starts-with, LIKE ends-with.
Starter idea: an in-browser sample table of nine countries (e.g. via sql.js or a JS array) with a query box.
Interactive demo idea: type a LIKE pattern and highlight which rows match, showing how % behaves at the start, end or both sides.
